pulls.title: Correct bot manager layer characterization (§2.1, §3.4, §6.3)
pulls.author: sthumma33
pulls.body:
Summary of Changes
This PR updates the architectural characterization of Bot Management Systems across §2.1, §3.4, and §6.3 of draft-skyfire-oauth-using-kyapay-tokens-00. It shifts the definition of bot managers from network/transport-layer filters (L3/L4) to inline application-layer (L7) systems.
Additionally, it reframes §6.3 around agent self-identification and policy-driven disposition:
Self-Identification Over Detection: Presenting a valid KYA token allows an agent to explicitly self-identify as automated up front. This settles the identification question and allows the bot manager to bypass redundant behavioral telemetry and fingerprinting heuristics.
Decoupling Identification from Admission: Token verification provides authenticated context (hid, apd, aid), but leaves admission as a site-configured policy decision (admit, rate-limit,  deny) rather than a mandated bypass.

pulls.title: Add a Token Size section setting the minimum a recipient must accept
pulls.author: skyfire-ankit
pulls.body:
This document defines the `KYAPay-Token` header field but says nothing about how large a value a recipient has to accept. Header field limits are set by deployment configuration and enforced at the origin, so a conformant token can be rejected before any claim is read, and an issuer has no size it can rely on.

**This is the recipient half.** The issuer-side guidance that makes the guarantee work is a companion pull request against `kyapay-token`. Neither is much use without the other, so please read them together.

### What it says

- **A recipient MUST accept a `KYAPay-Token` field value of at least 6144 octets**, applied to **the field value as a whole**, not to an individual token.
- **MUST NOT truncate** the field value, and MUST NOT validate a token reconstructed from a truncated one — a truncated JWT either fails signature verification or parses as a different, shorter token. Also MUST NOT treat a size rejection as a token-absent request, which would silently fall back to the bot policy.
- **SHOULD respond 431 rather than 400**, so a sender can tell a size limit from a malformed token and retry smaller.
- Adds `RFC6585` (normative) and `RFC9112` (informative).

### Why per field value rather than per token

§5.1 registers this field with `Structured Type: List` and permits more than one token per request, and RFC 9110 §5.2 lets a recipient coalesce multiple field lines into one. **A per-token minimum therefore bounds nothing at the origin:** two tokens at 6144 octets is 12,303 octets with the field name, against a single-field limit of roughly 8190 at common origin defaults.

This is not hypothetical for this document. §6.1 opens *"On receiving a request that carries one or more KYAPay tokens"*, and §6.10 makes the two-token case ordinary: KYA-only for discovery and cart-building, KYA plus PAY at checkout. So a per-token minimum would stop bounding anything at exactly the moment a payment happens.

### Why 6144

It is chosen against the smallest limit on the path, which is the **per-field limit at the origin**, not any intermediary in front of it. Common origin defaults for a single field are roughly an order of magnitude below the total-header limits of common CDNs, so a deployment that checks only its CDN's published limit can still be rejected behind it.

6144 plus the field name leaves room for the cookies, `User-Agent` and `Accept` an ordinary request already carries — and for `Signature` and `Signature-Input`, which §4.3 and §6.1 require whenever a token carries `cnf`. A larger minimum would not survive the hop the requirement exists to protect. 8192 plus the field name already exceeds it.

On the other side: a fully populated registered claim set is about 4200 octets serialized, so 4096 would reject a maximal conformant token. 6144 is the only value I could find that clears both constraints.

### Framing

Deliberately a requirement on the recipient and not a limit on the sender. A sender limit is unenforceable, would make existing deployments non-conformant, and — where a sender drops a claim to stay inside it — deprives the intermediaries of §6 of exactly the information they exist to act on.

Worth noting that MCP SEP-2243 considered a header size limit for the same reasons and declined one; every objection it raises is to a cap on senders, not to a floor on recipients, and it independently reports the same vendor range. Happy to add that as a reference if useful.

### Two things I have not done

- **No Document History entry**, because there is no `-02` block yet and the current rewrite of this document is not recorded in the history either. Glad to add both if you would like.
- **Numbering:** the section is placed as a subsection of the header field section, since it is a property of that field. Happy to move it if you would rather it sat in §8.

Opened as a draft for review.
